blocks.text: This review examined the state of the art across the three technical domains that underpin SentriZK and established a consistent picture of both progress and unresolved gaps. In the domain of confidentiality and authentication, the surveyed evidence shows that popular messaging applications operate only in an opportunistic end-to-end-encryption mode that defends against passive interception but remains vulnerable to active man-in-the-middle attacks through server-side key substitution, and that the authentication ceremonies meant to close this gap are optional and routinely defeated by human error [P1]. A concrete microservice implementation using Diffie-Hellman/ECDH key exchange with AES-256 confirms that strong message confidentiality against a compromised server is achievable, yet it lacks an authentication mechanism and on-device threat detection, leaving man-in-the-middle resistance dependent on fragile out-of-band trust [P5]. In the authentication domain, zero-knowledge proofs were shown to allow a prover to demonstrate possession of a secret without disclosing it, providing anonymity and man-in-the-middle resistance with lower overhead than PKI, with non-interactive zk-SNARKs offering succinct, fast-to-verify proofs [P6], [P7], and a real zk-SNARK identity-management deployment demonstrating password-less anonymous authentication on an EVM stack [P8]. In the threat-detection domain, deep-learning sequence models such as BiLSTM and LSTM were validated for insider-threat and anomaly detection [P2], [P3], [P9], while compact transformer and feature-based classifiers achieved high-accuracy phishing and smishing detection suitable for resource-constrained Android devices [P10], [P11], [P12]. Threat modeling for enterprise messaging further confirmed unauthorized access, data interception, and insider misuse as the dominant risk vectors [P4].

Across these domains a clear integration gap persists: confidentiality, privacy-preserving authentication, and intelligent threat detection have advanced largely in isolation, and no surveyed system unifies all three within a single mobile-first enterprise messenger. SentriZK is proposed to close this gap by combining established end-to-end encrypted transport (Diffie-Hellman key exchange with AES-256) [P5], non-interactive zk-SNARK (Groth16) authentication that removes error-prone manual fingerprint-verification ceremonies [P1], [P6], [P8], and on-device deep-learning threat detection deployed via TensorFlow Lite to avoid cloud latency and privacy leakage [P2], [P3], [P10], [P11]. As this work is a literature review at the design and review stage, no experimental performance is claimed for SentriZK; its contribution is the unifying conceptual architecture motivated by the gaps identified above.

Future work will proceed along several concrete directions. First, a functional Android prototype will be implemented to realize the three pillars end to end. Second, an evaluation plan will benchmark the threat-detection models against public datasets, including the CMU CERT corpus for insider-threat detection [P3] and public phishing and URL datasets for social-engineering detection [P11], [P12]. Third, on-device efficiency will be benchmarked, measuring inference latency, memory footprint, and battery impact under the composite efficiency criteria suited to resource-limited devices [P11]. Fourth, the zk-SNARK proof-generation overhead will be measured directly on mobile hardware, since prior work reports large proving keys and multi-second proof times that may be infeasible under tight mobile constraints [P7], [P8]. Fifth, a usability study will compare zero-knowledge-proof authentication against the manual authentication ceremonies whose human-error failures this review documented [P1]. Finally, the system's security posture will be validated against a formal threat model covering spoofing, data interception, and insider misuse [P4]. Together these steps will move SentriZK from a motivated design toward an empirically evaluated, privacy-preserving secure messaging platform.
